stories.headline: Gianluigi Donnarumma's Man City form 'no concern' - Enzo Maresca
stories.summary: Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca insists Gianluigi Donnarumma has his full backing and is not concerned about the goalkeeper's form.
stories.body:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca insists Gianluigi Donnarumma has his full backing and is not concerned about the goalkeeper's form.

Donnarumma was at fault for one of the goals conceded in City's 3-2 victory at RB Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday when he allowed a shot to beat him at his near post.

There were also a couple of other uncomfortable moments for the Italy No.1, who has made a number of uncharacteristic errors this season.

However, the former Paris Saint-Germain keeper did also make a fine save and Maresca is confident the 27-year-old will get back to his best.

"It's not a concern, but it's a mistake. We recognise that, he knows that it's a mistake, but now it's 48 hours [before] Nottingham Forest away, we need to be focused on that," Maresca said.

Asked if he was thinking of reviewing the position during the upcoming international break, Maresca told reporters at a news conference: "I'm not, to be honest. Seriously, at the moment I'm not thinking about the international break and goalkeeper situation because we are talking about a mistake.

"A few minutes before the mistake he has made a save that any keeper in the world is not going to do. So it's always a balance.

"Gigio knows that the first goal was not good but, again, he's going to do better."

Maresca accepted that his side needs to stop conceding "silly goals."

- Haaland tells Man City to 'step up' after netting winner in Leipzig

- Kuyt hails 'another miracle in Istanbul' after Fenerbahce beat former club Liverpool

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

City led twice through a Castello Lukeba own goal and Enzo Fernández header but were pegged back by Ridle Baku and Antonio Nusa. They hit back again to win through Erling Haaland in the 78th minute.

"I think that both goals are quite silly goals that we can avoid," the manager said. "I think we are creating, since day one, many chances in each game but we need to avoid conceding silly goals.

"But I'm new here. I need to know the players, they need to know me. It's four months that we are together. That's why I'm so happy, so confident, because we can only improve after this short period."

Maresca had warned before the game that his side could not only rely on Haaland to score their goals but the Norwegian was once again in the right place at the right time.

Haaland had been relatively quiet, touching the ball only 12 times before sliding on to Elliot Anderson's perfectly-weighted through ball to settle the contest.

It was his 14th goal of the season and his 62nd in 61 career Champions League appearances. It was also his 176th for City, putting him within one of equalling Eric Brook as the club's second-highest goalscorer.

Maresca said: "It's always important that he's in the game. We know that at any moment he can help us, he can score goals.

"We scored more goals with different players, and we created so many chances that unfortunately we missed, but again we're happy with the three points because Champions League away in Germany is always difficult."

stories.headline: Could Denver overcome a 'down' year from Nikola Jokic? Absolutely not
stories.summary: Denver's roster was never built to overcome any slippage from its three-time MVP.
stories.body:
For most of the past decade, the Denver Nuggets' NBA title hopes have hinged on the franchise's ability to assemble enough talent around Nikola Jokic.

That quest has taken memorable twists and turns: the evolution of Jamal Murray into bona fide sidekick, the franchise-changing trade for Aaron Gordon in 2021 and the emergence of Christian Braun and Bruce Brown during the 2023 championship run. Since that title, the capped-out Nuggets have slowly bled talent and failed to reach the conference finals in the past three seasons.

The constant focus on Denver's supporting cast has been a by-product of Jokic's dependability: The Serbian center has been the NBA's most consistent star of the 2020s, finishing first or second in Most Valuable Player voting for six straight seasons, ranking first in Player Efficiency Rating for six straight seasons and carrying Denver to eight straight playoffs and four straight 50-win campaigns.

But the Nuggets are suddenly facing an alarming question to begin 2026-27: Who are they if Jokic isn't consistently playing at an MVP level? So far, Denver has been a mediocre team that's still searching for its first statement win over top-quality competition.

Jokic seemingly entered the season poised to extend his run of exceptional basketball.

He's still just 31 years old and was coming off a season in which he averaged a triple-double and captained the NBA's most efficient offense. In September, Jokic claimed the top spot on NBA Rank, ESPN's annual projection of the league's top 100 players, and assured reporters that he plans to sign a contract extension with the Nuggets next summer.

And when Jokic found Cameron Johnson with an audacious behind-the-back, cross-court pass for a corner 3-pointer during an October preseason game, it was tempting to buy back into the Nuggets' chances and forget about April's demoralizing first-round exit against the Minnesota Timberwolves.

There was no obvious reason to expect Jokic's quality of play to diminish, but he's struggled at times to live up to his high standard during the first two weeks of the regular season. If the trend continues, Denver will be plunged into an existential crisis.

Why this isn't the same Joker
While all "small sample size" disclaimers apply, Jokic has gotten off to a slow start. Through seven games, he's shooting 50.4% from the field - his worst mark since 2017-18 -- and a career-low 21.9% from deep. His 26.1 Player Efficiency Rating (PER) is his lowest since his rookie season in 2015-16, and his 23.4 points per game represents his lowest output since 2019-20.

There's more cause for concern once you pop the hood. Jokic's average shot distance is 12 feet (tied for the longest of his career) because just 16% of his shots have come from the basket area (a career low) while 25% of his shots have come from beyond the arc (nearly a career high). Meanwhile, his free throw and offensive rebound rates are down sharply from last season and tracking toward career lows.

Jokic is still the only player in the league averaging 23 points, nine rebounds and nine assists, but his efficiency and forcefulness are clearly lagging behind his box score productivity. For now, Jokic ranks sixth leaguewide in PER and 15th in win shares after ranking first and second, respectively, by those metrics last season.

While a dominant Jokic led the Nuggets to a blowout win over the Raptors on Wednesday, he hasn't maintained that level of impact on winning or command of the paint on a night-to-night basis. By extension, the Nuggets' offense hasn't looked like the juggernaut we've come to expect.

The win over the Raptors, in which Jokic posted 32 points, 10 rebounds and 11 assists, provided hope that he is merely pacing himself to start a long campaign and that his poor outside shooting will prove to be a short-term slump. Nuggets coach David Adelman expressed confidence this week that Jokic's play will pick up with time.

"Some of the shots we're so accustomed to seeing that [Jokic] never misses, whether it's a jump hook or a 15-footer, all those kinds of things, they're coming," Adelman said after Monday's loss to the Portland Trail Blazers.

"This is a six-game sample size of one of the most efficient offensive basketball players that's ever lived. I'll die on that sword."

Why these aren't the same Nuggets

Denver's top-heavy roster was not designed to compensate for any slippage from Jokic. The Nuggets are 4-3 to start the season -- including an 0-3 mark against teams with winning records -- and have heard boos from their home crowd at Ball Arena. "I think those fans who booed us ... they're not welcome anymore," Jokic said after Denver's overtime win against the New Orleans Pelicans in the home opener.

Jokic's individual struggles have exposed the flaws around him: Gordon is not moving well after missing more than half of last season due to injury, Johnson continues to underperform, and a new-look second unit headlined by 37-year-old DeMar DeRozan has been outscored on a regular basis.

With Jokic drifting further from the hoop on offense to start the season, the Nuggets ranked 26th in points in the paint prior to their demolition of the Raptors. That looms as a potentially serious problem because Denver also ranks 28th in 3-point attempts per game. Adelman wants improvement in both facets, saying that he will continue making a "concerted effort" to establish Jokic in the post while also encouraging his role players to "get up more 3s."

But the Nuggets' longstanding winning formula -- an elite offense compensating for a so-so defense -- has looked shaky. Despite a strong start from Murray, Denver's offense ranks 11th entering Thursday. The Nuggets haven't ranked outside the top 10 since Jokic was a rookie.

"It's too much responsibility for [Jokic and Murray]," Adelman said Monday. "I have extreme trust in the others. They have to have trust in themselves."

Adelman's job description requires that he keep the faith in his role players, but he's working with a severely untested bench.

Rookie forward Trevon Brazile has been a pleasant surprise, but budget-friendly backups Marvin Bagley III, Bryce Hopkins, Alpha Diallo and Cam Whitmore have combined for only a handful of playoff appearances. Meanwhile, offseason additions DeRozan and Tyus Jones are both several years removed from having any real postseason impact.

All these new faces serve as a reminder of how few key figures remain from the Nuggets' 2023 championship team. Denver fired general manager Calvin Booth and coach Michael Malone less than two years after winning the title, and Jokic, Murray, Gordon, Braun and seldom-used big man Zeke Nnaji are the only players left from the 2022-23 roster.

Denver sought to replace Brown, Michael Porter Jr. and Peyton Watson with cheaper alternatives given that Jokic, Murray and Gordon all hold significant contracts, but those efforts have largely proven unsuccessful. Similarly, the Nuggets' recent draft history has featured more misses than hits.

Rather than replenishing Jokic's supporting cast with waves of young talent, Denver has settled for a new batch of free agent fliers every summer. Russell Westbrook, Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas, DeAndre Jordan and Reggie Jackson have all drifted in and out of Denver in recent years, making little impact.

Add it all up, and it's no surprise that Denver's bench ranks 28th in scoring and 23rd in net rating. That's a real drag for Jokic to overcome, even if he is able to recapture his top form.

Why Denver lacks real options to improve

To make matters worse, Denver's cap crunch won't ease any time soon.

If Jokic does sign an extension next summer (worth up to $360 million over five years), he will go on the long-term books next to Murray and Gordon, who are both under contract through 2028-29. Braun's five-year, $125 million extension, which just kicked in this season, is another quiet killer to the Nuggets' financial health.

They would struggle to get value in trades involving Gordon and Braun given their salaries, and they can't afford to part with Murray given his strong play and track record. None of Denver's younger players have played well enough to generate a significant trade return.

More importantly, if Jokic's impact continues to lag, the Nuggets will need to consider negotiating rather than simply handing him a maximum extension with a record average annual value of $72 million.

Signing a five-year extension next summer would carry Jokic through his age-36 season, and there is no recent precedent for a center playing at an MVP level that late in his career. Tim Duncan led a balanced San Antonio Spurs team to the 2014 championship in his age-37 season, but he earned only $10.4 million on a team-friendly discount that season -- a fraction of the maximum salary available to him.

Jokic's slow start has made it clear Denver lacks a succession plan should its franchise center encounter meaningful age-related decline or a significant injury. These Nuggets were constructed to support Jokic as best they could under the assumption that he would once again handle the heavy lifting. There's no rising superstar waiting to receive the baton, and Denver has already traded away its first-round picks in 2027, 2029 and 2032.

For Jokic and the Nuggets, something will have to give. There's no plausible path for Denver to re-sign Jokic to an enormous extension, make the necessary improvements to his supporting cast and avoid the NBA's second apron penalties. The Milwaukee Bucks reached a similar crossroads with Giannis Antetokounmpo last summer and elected to trade him to the Miami Heat and pursue a full rebuild.

To this point, Jokic has resisted applying pressure to overhaul the roster and has given no indication he wants to leave Denver.

While superstars such as LeBron James, Kevin Durant and Antetokounmpo have changed teams in recent years in hopes of improving their championship chances, Jokic could always follow the Dirk Nowitzki model. Nowitzki led the Dallas Mavericks to the 2011 title, then spent eight more seasons with the franchise even though he never won another playoff series.

Like Dallas with Nowitzki, Denver has plenty of good reasons to reward Jokic's loyalty as he ages. But this season has offered a glimpse at the organization's murky future: Jokic can only mask everything that's plaguing the Nuggets when he's playing at an MVP level.

When he's not, Denver's whole plan starts to fall apart.

stories.headline: Portugal, Man United, Real Madrid: Cristiano Ronaldo's long history of rows with coaches
stories.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international soccer with Portugal after being benched by coach Jorge Jesus. It is far from the first high-profile row of his career.
stories.body:
Editor's note: This has been updated after Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international soccer on Nov. 5, 2026.

Was it always going to end like this? Cristiano Ronaldo -- Portugal's greatest-ever player, who led them to victory at the 2016 UEFA European Championship, and won the UEFA Champions League and the Ballon d'Or five times in a glittering club career -- has called time on his international career.

Ronaldo, 41, walked away from the national team's camp last month after a row with coach Jorge Jesus. The Portugal boss insisted there was "no issue," but admitted mistakes in his handling of Ronaldo's role in the 2-1 win over Norway in the UEFA Nations League on Sept. 27, when he was an unused substitute.

Despite it seeming as though the coach and his captain had patched things up, Ronaldo confirmed on Thursday that he has played his last game for Portugal. However, an acrimonious end to his international career -- during which he has scored a men's record 146 goals -- could hardly be described as a shock.

- Live updates as Ronaldo retires from international football

- Ronaldo goal review: Why 982nd career strike should be an own goal

- Ronaldo goal tracker: 985 and counting on road to 1,000 career goals

Managing the transition when an aging superstar's performance level drops is never easy, and Ronaldo's role and impact -- positive and negative -- with Portugal had been debated for three successive major tournaments, in 2022, 2024 and 2026.

Throughout his 25-year career, Ronaldo has been involved in a series of headline-grabbing disagreements with managers, teammates and executives. With his latest drama seemingly resolved, here are some of the most high-profile previous examples.

Unhappy Ronaldo backs Blatter's insensitive "slavery" comparison (July 10, 2008)
Ronaldo's bid to leave Manchester United for Real Madrid that summer reached a new, histrionic high -- or low -- when Ronaldo echoed comments from then-FIFA president Sepp Blatter that keeping a player at a club against their will was comparable to "modern slavery." Ronaldo told Portugal's TV1: "It's true. I agree with what the president of FIFA said. I know what I want and what I would like. We have to see what happens. I do not know where I will begin next season." After five successful years at Old Trafford, Ronaldo was ready to move on, but United stood firm and the forward had to wait another season before his desired move to the Bernabéu was finally fulfilled.

Ronaldo subs himself off mid-game at Old Trafford (Dec. 6, 2008)
Ronaldo abruptly walked off the pitch -- and headed straight down the tunnel -- midway through Manchester United's 1-0 win over Sunderland at Old Trafford. The team were left playing with 10 men, as United's coaching staff rushed to organise an unexpected substitution. Manager Sir Alex Ferguson defended Ronaldo, saying he had received "a kick on the hip" and "there was no need for Cristiano to come to the bench" when he required immediate treatment, but it was clear that the player -- who had won his first Ballon d'Or earlier that week -- was increasingly willing to act out.

Derby withdrawal sparks bout of Ronaldo head-shaking (May 10, 2009)
Ronaldo's reaction to another substitution, this time in the heated atmosphere of a Manchester derby, was the latest sign of a growing estrangement between him and the club. He had put United ahead against City with an 18th-minute free kick -- the first goal of a 2-0 victory -- but when Ferguson opted to replace him with Paul Scholes on the hour, Ronaldo reacted furiously. He spent several minutes shaking his head in frustration on the bench in a very public, visible showing of discontent. That opening goal proved to be his last for the club for 12 years.

No celebrations for "sad" Ronaldo (Sept. 2, 2012)
Three years on from finally getting his desired move to Real Madrid, new signs of dissatisfaction emerged. Ronaldo had scored twice in a 3-0 LaLiga win over Granada, but was he happy? No, he wasn't. The lack of a goal celebration for either strike raised eyebrows, and his enigmatic postmatch comments set alarm bells ringing. "I'm sad because of a professional issue, and the club know it," Ronaldo revealed, mysteriously. "That's why I'm not celebrating my goals, because I'm not happy. The people here know why." The forward refused to elaborate, and an explanation for his ennui was never forthcoming. Ronaldo subsequently denied that money was the problem, but a bumper new contract that was eventually signed a year later might have helped.

Mourinho hits back at 'know-it-all' Ronaldo (June 5, 2013)
Ronaldo and manager José Mourinho were close when the two first worked together at Real Madrid, but -- in a developing trend -- their relationship was deteriorating by the end of the 2012-13 season, Mourinho's last at the Bernabéu. A dressing room bust-up after a Copa del Rey game with Valencia in January was the beginning of the end and by June, after dropping the forward for the last few games of the season, Mourinho was telling TV show Punto Pelota after leaving Los Blancos for a second spell at Chelsea that "Cristiano Ronaldo thinks he knows everything."

Ronaldo prefers Carlo to Rafa (Dec. 11, 2015)
Rafa Benítez was in charge at Real Madrid for only six months after replacing Carlo Ancelotti in June 2015 and getting sacked the next January, but there was still time for his relationship with Ronaldo to come under scrutiny. There was speculation that the player was unhappy with his manager's tactical approach, and Ronaldo's fulsome praise for predecessor Ancelotti -- calling him an "unbelievable person" and a "fantastic coach" (and, rather endearingly, a "big bear") whom he "wished to work with again" probably didn't help. Benítez insisted that he and the star were still "adapting to each other," but there wasn't time for that: A month later, Benítez was gone.

Ronaldo benched ahead of United move (Aug. 22, 2021)
Just a few days before the 2018 World Cup final (in which Portugal were not involved), Ronaldo's move to Juventus after nine years in Madrid was announced. But, after three years in Turin, Ronaldo was ready to move again. He was left out of the team for the Italian giants' Serie A opener for the 2021-22 season, a 2-2 draw at Udinese, after reportedly asking not to start the match. Juventus were insistent that the forward would stay, and Ronaldo himself had earlier branded reports linking him with a move back to Real Madrid as "disrespectful." However, just over a week later, he was on his way back to Manchester United on transfer deadline day having been heavily linked with joining rivals City.

Ronaldo is no fan of three at the back (Jan. 19, 2022)
If we've learned anything so far, it's that Ronaldo isn't keen on being substituted. Manchester United interim coach Ralf Rangnick found that out when looking to protect the team's 2-0 lead at Brentford by replacing Ronaldo with Harry Maguire and switching to a back three. Ronaldo wasn't a fan of the tactical change, throwing his coat to the ground as he departed, before Rangnick had to have a word. The reaction was "normal," Rangnick said, adding: "I said maybe when you're a head coach yourself you will hopefully make the same decision." The coach was proved right: United went on to win 3-1.

'Nonsense' reports of Maguire captaincy battle (Feb. 18, 2022)
A month later, Rangnick was called upon to dismiss claims of a rift between Ronaldo and defender Maguire as "absolute nonsense." The issue at stake was reportedly the United captaincy, with skipper Maguire feeling threatened by Ronaldo's outsized influence in the dressing room among younger players. Rangnick sought to quash that, saying, "I have never spoken with any player about a possible change of captaincy," and insisting Maguire would continue in his role until the end of the season.

Explosive interview forces Ronaldo's second Old Trafford exit (Nov. 13, 2022)
After a start to the season that saw Ronaldo's goals dry up and his first-team place rescinded by new manager Erik ten Hag, Ronaldo's clear frustration came to a head when on Oct. 21 when he refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham Hotspur, walked off down the tunnel and left Old Trafford before the final whistle -- something he also did during a preseason friendly with Rayo Vallecano.

His departure from United was finally sealed by a no-holds-barred interview with Piers Morgan. Ronaldo criticised just about everybody at Old Trafford -- saying he "didn't respect" Ten Hag, felt "betrayed" by senior executives, had "never heard of" Rangnick before his arrival and "zero progress" had been made since his first stint at the club. If the comprehensive takedown was designed to make his own position at United untenable, then it was a success, with the club agreeing to a departure by mutual agreement.

Ronaldo axed by Portugal, family reacts angrily (Dec. 6, 2022)
Ronaldo was dropped by coach Fernando Santos for Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 tie against Switzerland, and his replacement, Gonçalo Ramos, more than justified the decision, scoring a hat trick in a 6-1 win. Santos claimed the selection was based on "strategy," rather than Ronaldo's angry reaction to being substituted in Portugal's final group game, although Santos had previously said of his captain's outburst: "I didn't like it."

The Portuguese football federation (FPF) was then moved to deny reports that things had escalated before their quarterfinal against Morocco. "The FPF clarifies that at no time did the captain of the national team, Cristiano Ronaldo, threaten to leave the national team at any stage," it said in a statement.

Unsurprisingly, Ronaldo's omission didn't go well with the extended Ronaldo family. "What a shame not to have been able to enjoy the best player in the world for 90 minutes," partner Georgina Rodríguez said in a post on Instagram, and sister Elma Aveiro added: "It's a shame to humiliate a man who has given so much."

Ronaldo storms out of Portugal camp (Sept. 30, 2026)
And so here we are, waiting for Ronaldo to expand on the reasons for his latest walkout.

At the time of writing, we know that his exit followed a lack of minutes against Norway on Sunday, and then coach Jesus giving his version of events in a news conference three days later. Ronaldo, according to his own statement, then held "a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation." He also felt the need to wish his teammates "good luck, without exception" in Thursday's Nations League game with Denmark.

The last four years have been relatively calm by Ronaldo standards, with the forward scoring lots of goals -- and winning a couple of trophies -- with Al Nassr in the Saudi Pro League, and benefitting from a national team coach, Roberto Martínez, who backed him persistently at two major tournaments, despite growing criticism.

Jesus worked with Ronaldo at Al Nassr, but on this week's evidence, their relationship appears much less comfortable. We'll find out soon enough if it signals the end of a 23-year international career.

Ronaldo calls time on Portugal career (Nov. 5,2026)
After Portugal's matches ended in the Nations League for the international window, Ronaldo released a statement about what happened behind the scenes between him and Portugal coach Jesus, and what his future holds with the team.

In his statement, he accused Jesus of breaking two promises. The first was that the coach told Ronaldo that he should be ready to play 30 minutes against Norway -- where Portugal won 2-1 in Oslo -- at lunchtime on the day of the match. Ronaldo ended up not playing.

The second was that Jesus had agreed to address the issue in the press conference on the day prior to their match against Denmark in Copenhagen, following private conversations between him and Ronaldo.

The points that were to be brought up in the news conference ranged from "wanting Cristiano on the national team" to admitting he "made a mistake in having someone of the stature of Pelé or [Diego] Maradona warm up and then not putting him into game."

Jesus later said in the conference that "every player knows the coach makes the decisions" and that Ronaldo told him he would abide by whatever choices he makes, adding that the "rules are the same for everyone."

After that, Ronaldo left the team camp, and Portugal ended up winning the next two matches without him in the squad. The statement continued by saying that he "apologizes to his national team teammates for having left the camp" and says that "the consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation."

He closed it by saying that he "promises to have one or more farewell matches" and that "he will be available, as I always have been until today, to compete and win for our national team." However, we now know that will not be the case.

Portugal's upcoming matches against Denmark and Wales to close out their Nations League group will be their first without their captain, top scorer and greatest-ever player.

stories.headline: Best of MLB playoffs: Moments, games that defined October
stories.summary: A week after the Brewers completed their title run, here's what we won't soon forget from the 2026 postseason.
stories.body:
Whether you love dramatic finishes, thrilling moments or incredible individual performances, the 2026 MLB playoffs provided a little bit of everything.

A week after the Milwaukee Brewers lifted their first World Series championship trophy, we asked our MLB experts to pick the best single moments, games and series from the entire postseason -- along with their lasting October impressions.

From wild-card thrillers to World Series heroics, here is the best of the best from every round of the 2026 postseason.

What was the defining moment of the entire MLB playoffs?

Bradford Doolittle: As it turned out, I was at all the Brewers' playoff games except the two in San Diego. So I was there when Ty France launched a ball off the American Family Field ceiling, or some wires or whatever, and Jackson Chourio stuck with the play and caught it and the Brewers won. All through the rest of the postseason, Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy alluded to the play as Bob Uecker reaching down from the great beyond to swat that ball down to help the Brewers.

I can't get on board with that, but at the same time it was a moment when I felt like Milwaukee was destined to win. And all through the Brewers' run, it felt like so many borderline moments, whether resolved by luck or skill, went Milwaukee's way. You take baseball's best team and then give it the majority of the breaks and you have what we ended up with: a champion that went 11-2 en route to winning it all.

David Schoenfield: Given the strength of the top teams in the NL compared to the obvious weaknesses of the best AL teams, it felt like the NLCS between the Brewers and Dodgers was going to decide the eventual World Series champ. After losing Game 1 with Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers at least knew they had 2025 postseason hero Yoshinobu Yamamoto going in Game 2. Then came the bottom of the third inning and Jake Bauers' walk.

How can a walk be the defining moment of the MLB playoffs? Because it was a 12-pitch walk with Bauers grinding and battling and fouling off six pitches with a 3-2 count before finally drawing ball four. It wiped out Yamamoto. Christian Yelich followed with a go-ahead two-run single and Yamamoto was out of the game, unable to finish the inning. The Dodgers would actually retake the lead, but with Yamamoto gone early, the Brewers went back ahead against the Dodgers' second-line relievers. The Brewers had won games that Skubal and Yamamoto started. Neither would throw another pitch.

Jeff Passan: If anything encapsulated the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers, it was the fifth inning of Game 3 of the World Series. After Christian Yelich's excellent baserunning instincts saved the inning from ending on a force play at second, the Brewers rapped two-out hit after two-out hit en route to scoring eight runs and extending a 2-0 advantage to 10-0. This wasn't a moment, per se; it was 26 minutes of horror for Tampa Bay. And those minutes birthed a moment that's undeniable: the one in which the Rays understood just how different the Brewers really were.

What was the single best game of the entire MLB postseason?

Buster Olney: The Padres could've upended the Brewers' championship run in the division series between the two teams, and it looked like they might be in position to do that in Game 2, when they handed a 3-2 lead to the most feared closer in the game, Mason Miller.

The right-hander, asked to get the last six outs, zipped through three Milwaukee hitters in the eighth, needing only 12 pitches. But in the ninth, the Brewers' hitters did what they became known for in October: grinding through at-bats. With Miller suddenly struggling to command his fastball, Christian Yelich worked a walk, and after Yelich stole second, Sal Frelick walked. Then Miller's slider began to flatten out as his pitch count mounted, and pinch hitter Gary Sanchez stared him down for another walk, loading the bases.

Miller's pitch count had climbed over 30, and with his slider failing him, he leaned into his fastball against Jackson Chourio - and the 22-year-old swung confidently, aggressively. Miller's 40th pitch was a 101 mph fastball, and Chourio lashed a single to center to drive in the winning run. From that point forward, no one seriously threatened the Brewers.

Alden Gonzalez: This might not have been the best game of the postseason, per se, but it's one that shouldn't be lost to history. The Braves decided to push their ace, Chris Sale, back to Game 3 of the NLDS, a risky decision that felt calamitous after the Dodgers took Game 1.

Atlanta's hopes of maintaining a reasonable chance of winning the series would fall on the shoulders of its bullpen. And then Ray Kerr, a minor league journeyman who famously once worked at 7-Eleven, and Didier Fuentes, a 20-year-old who graduated to the big leagues much earlier than expected, combined for 19 of the Braves' 27 outs in an improbable victory, delivering 6⅓ innings of one-run ball.

The Braves went on to lose the next two games and were thus eliminated, but Game 2 of the NLDS was a reminder of what makes postseason baseball so great -- the surprises that define October, the guys you've never heard of who become heroes.

Jorge Castillo: The Brewers won the World Series in five games, but the matchup was plenty closer than that indicates. Three of the five games were decided by one run, including my pick for the best game of the postseason: Game 4 at Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay appeared on its way to getting swept when Cooper Pratt homered off Ian Seymour in the 12th inning to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead and move them within three outs of the first championship in franchise history. But the Rays, after not scoring since the fourth inning, scored two runs on an error and four straight singles without recording an out to keep their season alive.

The teams combined to use 15 pitchers. The Rays emptied their bench. Ben Williamson, the final player off that bench, delivered the walk-off single -- a ball that bounced off the artificial turf in front of home plate and into shallow right field. For one night, the Rays had hope.

What was the best series of the playoffs, from any round?

Jesse Rogers: If you can believe it, there were only two series that went the distance this October: The Braves beating the Phillies in the wild-card round and the Guardians outlasting the White Sox in their division series matchup.

The latter turned out to be one of the best of October as it featured a little bit of everything: Road teams winning the first four games, come-from-behind victories and dramatic moments -- like when Cleveland lefty Erik Sabrowski struck out Munetaka Murakami with the bases loaded in Game 5. Both fan bases were energized throughout the series, providing more energy in the building than some other contests in October. Oh, and Cleveland stormed back from 2-0 in the series to win it. It was a good one.

Olney: The Padres were the hottest team in the majors the last two months of the regular season, and in the divisional round, they faced the best team from 2026, the Brewers. It felt to a lot of folks in the game that the eventual champion would emerge from this series, and after some great moments -- Chourio's game-winning hit off Miller in Game 2, Garrett Mitchell intercepting a would-be home run in Petco Park -- Milwaukee survived the Padres and went 8-1 in its remaining postseason games.

Gonzalez: Buster is correct. There was no better series than Brewers-Padres. It lasted only four games, but every one of them contained a defining moment (don't forget Game 3, when Michael King, pitching two days after his start, took down the last two innings to save the Padres' season on a night when both Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller were unavailable).

The Brewers went on to sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS and breeze past the Rays in the final round. By the end, it was clear that the Padres were their biggest challenge. If any one moment goes the other way -- France's fly ball, Chourio's at-bat, King's appearance, Machado's fly ball -- we might be looking at a different World Series champion right now.

What is your lasting takeaway of this MLB postseason?

Passan: The return of small-market, low-payroll teams to the apex of the sport amid a labor negotiation in which the owners continue to suggest small-market, low-payroll teams can't compete in the current environment. The league's point about the recent history of World Series participants coming from larger markets and payrolls is fair, but multiple owners, speaking on the condition of anonymity, acknowledged that the Brewers and Rays facing off in the World Series did little to help reinforce their argument that a salary cap's main purpose would serve competitive balance.

Schoenfield: The perception -- incorrect -- that the Brewers were some scrappy, small-ball team that punched above its weight and slapped the ball around to victory. Nonsense. Yes, the Brewers have made some wonderful moves through the years to obtain players other teams didn't want, especially flipping Josh Hader for Robert Gasser (their Game 3 starter) and Esteury Ruiz, who was later traded for William Contreras. They got closer Trevor Megill for nothing, and Jake Bauers emerged off the scrap heap to have a star turn in 2026.

But this team has talented players up and down the roster: Brice Turang was a first-round pick in 2018, Garrett Mitchell in 2020, Sal Frelick in 2021. Yelich, Andrew Vaughn and DL Hall were first-round picks by other organizations. Cooper Pratt was a sixth-round pick, but regarded as a first-round talent and signed for second-round money. Jacob Misiorowski was a second-round pick. Jackson Chourio was the No. 2 prospect in the game. Luis Lara is a 21-year-old speedster who can run everything down in the outfield.

Yes, the Brewers have a different style -- they had the highest ground ball rate in the majors -- but they still hit the ball hard. They had the seventh-highest average exit velocity in the regular season and the third-most balls hit at 100-plus mph. They draw walks -- second-most in the regular season and 15 more than their opponents during the postseason. Most of the position players can run as well. They draft athletes and develop them and get their pitchers to throw harder or throw more strikes.

They actually struck out a few more times than their opponents during the playoffs. Sure, they hit "only" 13 home runs in 14 playoff games -- but they outhomered their opponents 13-4. They won with scouting, player development, execution, plate discipline and enough home run power. They have good baseball players. That's why they won.

Doolittle: As soon as the World Series matchup was set, I was fixated on the television ratings. I wasn't so much concerned with comparisons to the past two years, which both featured ideal conditions to produce big ratings. I was really curious how they would compare to 2023 -- the Rangers-Diamondbacks matchup that did not fare well in the ratings game. It was a short series, like this one, and also didn't feature markets favored by television, or at least as I understand the subject.

This series by all accounts fared way better than that one, with around 11.7 million viewers on average as compared to around 9.1 million in 2023. Here is my contention: People were thrilled by this matchup and this was true because of how these teams play baseball and, most crucially, because they were the respective top seeds in their leagues. It was the same matchup we would have gotten if we were still using the format in place from 1903 to 1968. In 2023, by contrast, we were watching a 5-seed against a 6-seed.

I think this matters -- a lot -- and I think favoring a format that rewards regular season excellence should be paramount when we consider such things going forward.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Previewing Preds-Avs, Canes-Isles, nine other Thursday games
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
Hockey fans should be ready for another busy night of action Thursday, with 11 games on the schedule after just four on Wednesday.

There are a number of interconference matchups on tap again, but two particularly intriguing ones are intradivisional with the Hurricanes visiting the Islanders and the Avalanche hosting the Predators.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Utah Mammoth at Montreal Canadiens

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | UTA -112, O/U: 6.5

Perhaps an under-the-radar legit Stanley Cup Final matchup possibility? Stathletes projections gives this pairing a 0.75% chance, which is 39th highest.

These two teams are both still in their "rising powerhouse" phase, driven by a number of young players in critical roles including Utah's Logan Cooley and Dylan Guenther, as well as Montreal's Lane Hutson and Jacob Fowler.

The Mammoth head to la belle province after a 3-2 win over the Leafs, while the Habs are hoping for a better result than Tuesday's, when they relented four goals in 2:08 at the tail end of the third period in an OT loss to the Jets.

Vegas Golden Knights at Detroit Red Wings

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -142, O/U: 5.5

The Wings have shaken off a rough start and are now in the thick of the playoff race in the East, focusing on on-ice success and avoiding the off-ice drama playing out with Dylan Larkin.

Vegas was one of three teams on Larkin's initial preferred list, although that cohort has since expanded to 10 teams. The Knights enter this game in a battle with the Oilers atop the Pacific, and we suppose any team could use a player of Larkin's caliber in the lineup.

This is the first time these two teams will play this season, after the Golden Knights won both matchups in 2025-26.

Chicago Blackhawks at Tampa Bay Lightning

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TB -380, O/U: 6.5

Speaking of stars requesting a trade, reigning Hart Trophy winner Nikita Kucherov informed the Lightning that this will be his last season with them, and that he wants to be traded. Coach Jon Cooper said that Kucherov remains "committed" to the team amid the request, and the fans in Tampa support him.

Oh and by the way, in the two games since the request was made, Kucherov has five assists.

It's not clear that the Blackhawks are a front-runner to land Kucherov, and they enter this game without two key contributors (defenseman Bowen Byram and winger Patrick Kane). Can the healthy Hawks pull off the big upset against an inspired Kucherov & Co.?

St. Louis Blues at New Jersey Devils

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NJ -192, O/U: 5.5

After an epic 4-3 shootout win over the Oilers on Tuesday, the Devils welcome a Blues team to Newark that is still finding its footing.

Four of the Blues' five leading scorers are 25 or younger -- Dylan Holloway, Jimmy Snuggerud, Mason McTavish and Philp Broberg -- and Joel Hofer has taken command of the crease and posted top-10 marks in both goals-against average (2.39) and save percentage (.918).

On the Jersey side, new goaltending addition Connor Hellebuyck is a perfect 3-0-0 to start his Devils career, stopping 54 of 60 shots he's faced since coming over from Winnipeg in trade. And forward Jack Hughes is off to an impressive start with 19 points in 15 games, on pace for 106 in an 84-game season.

Carolina Hurricanes at New York Islanders

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+/Disney+/Hulu) | CAR -166, O/U: 5.5

The Canes have been rolling over opponents this season, to the tune of a 12-3-2 record and plus-24 goal differential, both tops in the NHL.

Goaltender Pyotr Kochetkov has leveled up right before our eyes, starting the campaign 10-1-0 with a 1.64 GAA and .922 SV%. Meanwhile, oft-underrated Sebastian Aho is a top-10 scorer, with 21 points through 17 games.

Of course, the Isles also have a top-10 netminder in their crease in the form of Ilya Sorokin. Can he improve upon his most recent start against the Canes this past Apr. 4, when he allowed four goals on 40 shots?

Philadelphia Flyers at New York Rangers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYR -155, O/U: 6.5

The New York-Philadelphia rivalry runs deep across all sports, and that obviously includes all of the classic Rangers-Flyers tilts throughout the years.

The Blueshirts have the upper hand for now, holding down the No. 3 spot in the Metro while the Flyers are in the Eastern Conference basement. But this will be a showcase game for young talent on both squads, particularly given how leaky the goaltending has been for both teams.

Pay special attention to Philly's Trevor Zegras (14 points in 17 games) and Matvei Michkov (13 in 17), along with New York's Adam Fox (19 in 16) and Alexis Lafreniere (16 in 16).

Boston Bruins at Pittsburgh Penguins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | PIT -112, O/U: 6.5

While the Flyers are in the conference basement, their in-state rivals are only ahead in the standings based on the games played tiebreaker. So no, things are not going super well in the Steel City, entering this game following three straight losses.

With that backdrop, it's not super great that the Bruins area headed to town. Boston is 11-4-1, and appears to be firing on all cylinders in all facets of the game; the B's are eighth in the league in scoring (3.56 goals per game) and fourth in goals allowed per game (2.38) thanks to a stellar start from Jeremy Swayman.

On the plus side for the Penguins, they have a 4-1-1 record at home this season, so perhaps the friendly environment can help get them back on the winning side.

Dallas Stars at Columbus Blue Jackets

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | DAL -130, O/U: 5.5

This is the second and final matchup between these two clubs in 2026-27 -- well, unless they meet in the Stanley Cup Final -- after the Stars won 3-1 on Halloween.

The notable part about that prior matchup is that there were not one but two buzzer beaters! Thomas Harley scored with 0.2 seconds left in the first period to give Dallas a 2-0 lead, then Artttu Hyry sealed the deal with an empty-netter with 0.3 seconds left in the third.

It'll be tough to top that matchup for drama, but each team has a player coming off a big performance into this showdown: Jason Robertson scored a natural hat trick in the Stars' 6-5 win over the Capitals while Charlie Coyle had two goals in the Blue Jackets' 7-2 win over the Avs (while wearing their cool new Hometown Remix uniforms).

Vancouver Canucks at Winnipeg Jets

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WPG -230, O/U: 6.5

Speaking of timely goals being scored, the Jets authored one of the most epic comebacks in the history of all sports in their recent win over the Canadiens, scoring four times in the span of 2:08 in the third period, then winning in OT. Do they have anything special in store for the Canucks on Thursday?

Vancouver recently broke a 10-game losing streak with a thrilling 6-5 OT win over the Ducks ... only to lose the next three games.

This is the first of three matchups between the teams after Winnipeg swept the 2025-26 season series 3-0.

Anaheim Ducks at Edmonton Oilers

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | EDM -198, O/U: 6.5

After the shootout loss in Jersey, the Oilers are back home to take on a Ducks team that they beat 5-2 back on Oct. 7.

That game looked like it was going to be the Beckett Sennecke Show, with the Ducks forward netting two first-period goals to give his team the edge after one frame. Instead, it became yet another episode of the Connor McDavid-Leon Draisaitl-Evan Bouchard Show, as the terrifying trio had a hand (or two... or three) in five straight goals for Edmonton.

Ah, but there could be another character who takes center stage in this one; Anaheim's Cutter Gauthier scored a hat trick in the team's win over Vancouver on Tuesday, and could have more tricks up his sleeve in this one.

Nashville Predators at Colorado Avalanche

9:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+/Disney+/Hulu) | COL -238, O/U: 6.5

In the nightcap, the Avs welcome the Preds to Ball Arena looking for vengeance after Nashville won 6-2 on Oct. 25.

Steven Stamkos and Ryan O'Reilly each had two goals in that game, which was more than enough for Justus Annunen, who saved 19 of 21 shots.

On the Colorado side, Nathan MacKinnon is riding a six-game scoring streak, with 11 total points in that span (three goals, eight assists).
