stories.headline: Run, Man United, run: How preseason fitness can hinder Premier League form
stories.summary: Man United rank poorly compared to other Premier League teams in every running statistic presented, and there is no way to rectify it this season.
stories.body:
Manchester United are in crisis (again). Manager Michael Carrick's position has come under severe scrutiny following a terrible set of results and a public falling-out with his best player and captain, Bruno Fernandes. A run of three defeats -- 4-1 to Como, 3-0 to AFC Bournemouth and 2-0 to Chelsea -- brought about fresh discussion over the club's direction - although the dramatic 3-2 victory over Roma in the Champions League provided some respite.

Central to those discussions was the club's perceived fitness levels. It has been a theme all season as weekly graphics are dished out on social media that show the Red Devils ranking toward the bottom of the Premier League for almost every running statistic: distance covered, sprinting, high speed running, and more.

It's been this way since the beginning of the season, when summer signing Youri Tielemans said in an interview with former United defender Rio Ferdinand that their preseason training had been almost exclusively "ball work" and involved very little running. Then United promptly lost to newly promoted Hull City on the opening weekend.

Tottenham Hotspur have also been in crisis. Three wins on the bounce has hinted at the green shoots of recovery, but they failed to win a game before the three-week October international window, with manager Roberto De Zerbi suggesting his side lacked "physical condition" and vowing to try to help fix it during that extended break.

Running and fitness alone do not win games, but now that the season is underway, how fixable is this for these two teams? And in United's case, how concerned should we really be with those damning statistics?

The stats are grim
It is crucial to note that running data is highly contextual, does not necessarily correlate to success, and must be interpreted in conjunction with the team's tactical framework and style of play.

That being said, this, via Gradient Sports, looks bad.

United rank poorly compared to other Premier League teams in every running statistic presented, and they're bottom of the pile for average max speed. The gap between United and the team that has covered the most distance is 44.6 km, while the gap to the top sprinters is 5.34km.

Spurs are -- for the most part -- distinctly middling, although being 16th for distance covered is likely what's irking De Zerbi, a manager who strongly incorporates data into his preparations and thinking.

Now to reiterate, running more does not correlate to winning more, or vice versa. The team that has covered the most distance so far this season: Fulham, who are 15th. And the team who have sprinted the most: 14th-placed Ipswich Town.

So to interpret this properly, teams' tactical styles must be considered, as they condition the type and amount of running you do.

"Physical preparation hinges on your game model," Dave Carolan, a 30-year veteran of sports science in the Premier League and Football League, explains to ESPN. "How are your tactics physically expressed? Training is designed and used to develop the qualities you desire."

Teams who press high, chase the ball and defend big spaces are likely to clock up more kilometers run; teams who set up in a deep defensive block and counterattack frequently will probably sprint more. Conversely, averaging a huge amount of possession per game can sometimes skew physical statistics, as you may run less -- and you'll almost certainly sprint less -- when you have lots of the ball.

Through nine Premier League gameweeks, Newcastle United, Bournemouth and Brentford are among the top sprinters -- three teams noted for either high pressing or an intense, combative style. Fulham, who play at a high tempo in attack and leave big spaces in defense, have run the most overall.

All of this checks out, stylistically speaking.

So how do we define Man United and Spurs?

Man United have averaged 55% average possession across nine league games so far. It's an uptick on last season's average of 51.6%, but it's also a small sample size in which they've played against two of the four lowest possession teams in the division (Hull average 33.2%; Ipswich Town average 45.5%).

Carrick clearly wants his team to get their foot on the ball, but with the speed of Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford & Co. up front, they rightly open the door to attacking quickly, too.

The Red Devils' PPDA (how many opposition passes you allow before a defensive intervention of some kind) is 12.8, right in the middle of average for the league. They've also forced 56 high turnovers this term, which is the 11th-most in the league. In fact, they're the very definition of middling in just about every pressing statistic available.

This seems to have caused some consternation among some of the players; Fernandes' comments after the 4-1 defeat to Como in the UEFA Champions League would certainly suggest that. "I think we started on the wrong foot again, and they scored very early," he said. "Not much pressure on the ball, not many good movements without the ball. Sometimes when you give too much of the ball to these teams, they get confidence. It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man."

As a result, he was dropped for the defeat against Bournemouth.

But he was right. United are not covering the ground and are not successfully committing to an effective press. They're also not averaging such a huge amount of possession that their low sprint distances (and, to an extent, their low distance covered) can be easily justified.

Spurs, on the other hand, are without a doubt a high-possession, high-pressing side. De Zerbi has always coached this style and while the 2025-26 season saw him arrive in March to try and stop the club's slide to relegation, often doing whatever he could to survive by any means necessary, his desired tactical footprint is starting to show this term.

Spurs average 63.2% possession -- only Man City (64.5%) average more -- while they're the lowest in the division in PPDA (8.5) and second for high turnovers (88). A team as proactive as this might well be expected to rank quite highly in running metrics, especially sprinting, but they're average at best.

Watch a handful of Spurs' first Premier League games this season and you'll see why. They started most of them in thunderous fashion, swarming all over their opponents as they sought an early goal, but then too often failed to find it and, after 30 minutes or so, faded physically.

That resulted in mistakes, concessions and losses. The defeats to Aston Villa (3-2) and Newcastle United (2-0), in particular, followed this pattern, and are likely what De Zerbi was referring to when he branded his side unfit.

Can it be fixed?
It's all well and good preaching an energetic, high-tempo playing style, but the key question is: Do you actually have the physical capacity to do it?

Multiple sources confirmed to ESPN that Man United and Spurs were among a small group of Premier League clubs who did little to no dedicated conditioning work over the summer. Tielemans effectively confirmed that to be the case at United in August, while De Zerbi admitted his Tottenham side weren't where they should be physically four games in.

And here's the tricky bit: It's really hard to recover from this -- especially for clubs with busy schedules.

"It is fundamentally very difficult to change your physical condition in the middle of the season -- especially in the Premier League, the most physically demanding league in the world," Carolan tells ESPN. "These squads are built full of international players and you have packed schedules with European games. You cannot do major physical preparation if you're always MD-1 or MD-2 (matchday minus one/two -- one or two days before the game). Opportunities to do added work are limited."

At the elite level, physical preparation for the season starts before preseason; it begins in the offseason, where players are away from the club, but are typically given running programs to follow so that they can report in a certain condition.

"Traditionally, we use the offseason as a foundational period. You build strength, endurance, speed, power, and repeatable sprinting ability. This is core aerobic work, at a high intensity," Carolan says. "Then preseason goes on top of the foundation. [From a physical perspective], you can go from a 5 (out of 10) to an 8, but you can't go from a 3 to an 8."

Common consensus among experts ESPN spoke to suggests players can gain roughly 20% in fitness through preseason, but any more is a stretch. Coming in undercooked can set you back for a whole year.

"If the players don't do the work in the close season, you probably can't get to the level you want," Carolan agrees. "Then if you have a disrupted or poor preseason, it's potentially a recipe for disaster."

This is particularly relevant to United, whose schedule is chock full due to their participation in the Champions League. Where is Carrick (or anyone who might replace him) going to find the time to ask his squad to put the hard yards in?

Equally important is whether the players truly have the capacity to improve. Tielemans, Kobbie Mainoo and Andrey Santos are among the least athletic midfielders in the league (all rank in the bottom half or towards the bottom of the Premier League in Gradient's sprinting and high-speed running metrics). It's a similar situation in defense, where Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martínez rank towards the bottom of their position group for sprinting and high-speed running, too.

Put simply: this is an unathletic team, so how athletic can they actually be, even at their peak?

Spurs at least have a chance at rectifying this; with no midweek commitments, there are windows to add in some heavy conditioning work. There's also some obvious physical prowess in the squad to be unlocked: Sandro Tonali is a formidable athlete, Mohammed Kudus and Sávio are extremely dynamic, while Micky van de Ven is one of the fastest center backs in the league.

De Zerbi seemed to suggest he used October's international break to try to address some of this, as a decent chunk of his players weren't called up for international duty. Though, they're starting from a long way back.

The extended 2026 FIFA World Cup, which ate all the way into mid-July, is a factor but not an excuse: Every other top club faced the same issue, and the number of minutes Spurs' players clocked at the tournament (3,232) pales in comparison to Bayern Munich (5,931) or Paris Saint-Germain (4,651); closer to home, Arsenal's players racked up over 4,000 and Man City just under 5,000, but they're both in fine physical fettle.

More problematic was their choice of preseason tour, as Spurs flew about as far as possible, to Australia and New Zealand, and in doing so traded valuable conditioning time for time sitting on planes. It is little wonder they entered the season undercooked and opened with a 3-0 loss to Brentford.

For Spurs, things are potentially fixable, and they are starting to turn things around. But the same can't be said for Man United, whose players only had 2,533 minutes of action at the World Cup, and must now find a way to compensate and compromise for the next six months -- or else the current speculative talk of a relegation battle could become an unfortunate reality.

stories.headline: Francona brings in former assistant Joe Torres as Reds pitching coach
stories.summary: Joe Torres has been hired as the Cincinnati Reds' pitching coach after spending the past five seasons with the Cleveland Guardians as their assistant pitching coach.
stories.body:
CINCINNATI -- Joe Torres has been hired as the Cincinnati Reds' pitching coach after spending the past five seasons with the Cleveland Guardians as their assistant pitching coach.

Reds manager Terry Francona had Torres on his Guardians coaching staff in 2022 and '23. Before joining the major league staff, Torres spent five seasons coaching in Cleveland's minor league system.

The 44-year-old Torres was the 10th overall pick in the 2000 amateur draft by the Los Angeles Angels. He also spent time with the White Sox, Dodgers, Rangers and Rockies before retiring in 2013.

Torres inherits a staff that includes Chase Burns, who was fourth in the National League with 15 wins and ninth in strikeouts (185) last season. The Reds, though, had the third-highest ERA in the majors (4.83), with their starting staff at 4.97.

Cincinnati finished last in the NL Central with a 75-87 record after making the postseason in 2025.

stories.headline: Wysh List: Seven teams that could win Nikita Kucherov derby
stories.summary: The hockey world was shocked by the Lightning star asking for a trade. Here's who could make a deal happen.
stories.body:
The hockey world was shocked by Tampa Bay Lightning star Nikita Kucherov asking for a trade last week, as well as his decision to not sign a new contract with the team after this season.

(OK, maybe his general manager wasn't shocked, for reasons we'll get into later.)

There were different jolts within that shock. That last season's most valuable player suddenly becoming available, either as a free agent next summer or more immediately through a trade this season, was a jolt. The Lightning losing that Hart Trophy winner, which might slam shut a Stanley Cup contention window that was barely cracked open, was a jolt.

It's a new milestone in the "player empowerment" movement, albeit a player who is a pending free agent rather than one leaving during a long-term deal. Or as Tampa Bay teammate Brandon Hagel put it, with a nod toward Connor Hellebuyck and Dylan Larkin: "It's not like he committed here for eight years and asked out two years into it."

(Thus reinforcing the notion that Hagel hates anything, and anyone, associated with Team USA with the fury of a thousand burning suns, save for Jake Guentzel.)

But the biggest jolt of all was that any of this was happening to begin with: Kucherov wanting out, and the Lightning and GM Julien BriseBois having allowed it to reach this point.

"It's a shock the way things have been handled there," one former teammate of Kucherov's told me this week. "He's the kind of guy where the minute July 1 hits, you'd expect he'd have a deal done."

There was no deal in the summer or in training camp. Kucherov said he and the team have had only two conversations about his contract in the four months leading to his trade request.

My colleague Kevin Weekes reported the Lightning's first offer to Kucherov was around $13 million annually, making him the only current Tampa player with a cap hit higher than $10 million. Weekes said that BriseBois went all the way up to $15 million annually after the NHL's big spending summer, as the Ducks matched Leo Carlsson's offer sheet ($18 million AAV) and the Avalanche signed Cale Makar to new deal with a record $20.8 million cap hit.

Sources told me earlier this year that Kucherov was seeking an average annual value north of $17 million, which is the AAV on Kirill Kaprizov's contract with the Minnesota Wild. Multiple reports said Kucherov was now seeking a contract of six years and $20 million annually after the NHL financial landscape shifted in the summer.

He turns 34 next June. If age is a concern for the Lightning, it shouldn't be. First off, Kucherov isn't exactly a speedster, so any decline in his skating won't impact a pair of the best hands in the league (and a brain to match). Second, every current and former teammate I've spoken to about his condition raves that he'll be productive deep into his late 30s.

No, the concern for the Lightning is the compensation, what it does to their salary structure and how it affects BriseBois's cap flexibility. Remember what the GM said when he let Steven Stamkos walk? That meeting his contract demands "would not being putting ourselves in the best position to chase championships moving forward."

(And let's not lose sight of how that whole situation with Stamkos in 2024 plays on the mind of Kucherov.)

BriseBois and Lightning coach Jon Cooper had a meeting with Kucherov and his agent Dan Milstein in Nashville last Friday. At 6:49 p.m. ET that night, Elliotte Friedman of Sportsnet sent out his breaking news on Kucherov's trade request. At 9:35 p.m., the Lightning released a statement from BriseBois that said "we unequivocally have no intention of trading Nikita."

On Saturday, Cooper told reporters: "Kuch is 100% a part of this team. He wants to be a part of this team for this season, and he is committed to be with the group that loves him and the group he loves."

On Monday, Kucherov finally met with reporters to say that "it was never about the money to me. It was more about poor communication and respect," while adding "for now, I'm part of the team, and I will do everything I can to help my teammates win."

It was interesting to see the reaction to Kucherov asking out. I saw a lot of sentiment online that he had done the Lightning a solid by clearly communicating his intention to not sign and pushing them along to acquire assets for him out the door. I don't know if fans are being "player empowerment-pilled" or they're just relieved to see a pending unrestricted free agent declaring his desire to leave rather than a guy in the middle of a long-term contract, but there was a lot of sympathy for Kucherov.

My initial reaction was that it was understandable moment of petulance.

He's a superstar who has helped lead the Lightning to a decade of success, and suddenly he's not feeling the love at a critical contractual time. That's understandable, as is communicating that he doesn't intend to re-sign. The petulance is making this all public, which hurts the Lightning's negotiating leverage and creates a giant distraction for those teammates he's trying to help win.

Unless, of course, this is exactly how BriseBois wanted it to play out.

Here's a theory I heard from two separate NHL sources in the last week: BriseBois has shown a propensity for moving on from players who would have required a hefty commitment of years and money. Players such as Alex Killorn, Yanni Gourde and, of course, Stamkos.

If BriseBois also wanted to move on from Kucherov, there would have been more blowback on him and the franchise than with any other player who previous bolted, as a Hart Trophy winner. Despite a 40-goal season, there were those who felt Stamkos was in decline at the time of his departure. Not so with Kucherov. Trading him or walking away would be extremely unpopular.

So the theory goes that BriseBois ignored negotiations and hospitality with his star winger, while sticking to his financial benchmarks, to force Kucherov and his agent to state their intentions and demand a trade. Now, it's a general manager granting a player's trade request rather than proactively dealing him. There is a difference.

Is this plausible?

"I wouldn't put it past him," one former Lightning player said of BriseBois.

When asked about that theory, an NHL executive said: "Yeah, I don't buy that. Julien has always had a price and will grind guys down to get it. He'll walk them to free agency and have them decide they want to stay for that price."

Under that scenario, Kucherov would remain with the Lightning through the season. I still think that's the most likely scenario. There's zero chance they get anything close to equal value for Kucherov. They'd essentially be trading any chance of winning a championship along with him. So it's plausible that the two alphas coexist until it's time to either take what the Lightning are offering or go elsewhere to find that $20 million AAV payday.

But I keep coming back to that BriseBois statement: "We unequivocally have no intention of trading Nikita."

Intentions are not concrete. "Good intentions" literally means the desire to do something helpful. It doesn't mean you've done it.

So perhaps there's a chance for a trade. At the very least, there's a chance for Kucherov to leave as a free agent. If he does go via either route, here are six teams that would be fascinating winners in the Nikita Kucherov derby:

Montreal Canadiens
How many boxes do the Canadiens check for Kucherov? They have coach Martin St. Louis, his former teammate. They have Ivan Demidov, a young Russian star who shares an agent with Kucherov. They have offensive dynamos with whom Kucherov can play, whether it's up with Nick Suzuki or across from Demidov or in front of Lane Hutson. They're also a meticulously managed team under the salary cap, setting themselves up for a giant swing like this for an ascendant team that made the conference finals last season.

If there's a knock on this move, it's that the Canadiens have more pressing needs, especially at center. But it's Nikita Kucherov. You make exceptions when it's Nikita Kucherov. (A trade scenario I've been toying with: Dylan Larkin won't go to Montreal; Nikita Kucherov probably doesn't sign in Detroit; so, the Canadiens send the trade package they've offered for Larkin to the Lightning for Kucherov, and the Bolts then send it to the Red Wings for Larkin. Two off-ice dramas solved at once!)

Utah Mammoth
The Mammoth also made immediate sense. Defenseman Mikhail Sergachev is Kucherov's former Lightning teammate, one of his closest friends and is signed through 2030-31. Like Montreal in the East, they're on their way up in the Western Conference and should remain there give the age of their core and the reinforcements in their prospect pipeline. He could play with Clayton Keller, who has a 90-point season to his credit, or he could play with someone such as Logan Cooley and elevate him to superstar status.

One of the things Kucherov cherishes about playing in Tampa is not having to be a front-facing talent for the franchise. He just kind of does what he does, without multitudes of media interviews and appearances at car dealership openings. One assumes that's the kind of existence he could have in Utah, should he choose that destination.

Vegas Golden Knights
By law, we must include the Golden Knights if a superstar player could become available in free agency or via trade. They'd have to bury a few contracts in the desert to make it happen -- and adding Kucherov's salary would make them a perilously top-heavy team at forward against the cap.

But they're a contender, they have Ivan Barbashev as a countryman and a Milstein client, and Kucherov would have the likes of Jack Eichel and Mitch Marner with whom to vibe. Oh, and no state income tax. That too.

Dallas Stars
Another no-tax state, in case Kucherov is wrong and it's a little about the money. The Stars literally have an entire Nikita Kucherov cap hit coming off their books next summer at the forward spot. Jason Robertson and Tyler Seguin are unrestricted free agents. That's $21.85 million in cap space that could open up for a player reportedly seeking just below that.

Seguin certainly isn't coming back at that cap hit, if he's back at all. What the Stars and Robertson end up doing in the long term is anyone's guess. The way Dallas has treated Robertson makes it look like BriseBois was on one knee reading Kucherov poetry by comparison. Would Mikko Rantanen move to the middle to play with Kucherov? Wouldn't you?

New York Rangers
Stop me if you've heard this one before. The Rangers send a letter to their fans declaring that the franchise is going to make some painful personnel decisions and enter into a retooling phase. The next year, they sign a Russian-born superstar winger to a massive free agent contract to expedite the rebuild and join the star Russian goalie that was, at the time, on his way.

Now, Artemi Panarin was in his late 20s when he signed with the Rangers while Kucherov will be 34. But this is the kind of cheat code move that New York is famous for making. They prepare the fans for pain and then add a big name in lights on Broadway while flexing their financial and cultural muscle. They have the cap space next season. Having Igor Shesterkin doesn't hurt, either.

(Of course, there's another Russian goalie by the name of Ilya Sorokin on the New York Islanders, where former Lightning assistant GM Mathieu Darche is the general manager. Let's not discount that possibility, either.)

Chicago Blackhawks
Desperate times call for $20 million average annual value contract offers to two-time league MVPs. GM Kyle Davidson isn't long for that chair if things don't start to turn it around in Chicago, where the Blackhawks were 31st in the league after 15 games. They do have a star player for Kucherov in Connor Bedard, who would probably submit to some dark magic ritual to conjure this free agent signing.

Or, perhaps, a trade: What collection of young players would the Blackhawks move for Kucherov that the Lightning would identify as their next Brandon Hagel? Chicago is so terrible that Kuch might never extend there anyway, but Davidson needs to back up the truck and find out.

Let's add a seventh team here: The Tampa Bay Lightning.

As one NHL source put it, the beef is between Kucherov and BriseBois. Not the teammates. Not the fans. Not the coach, at least from what I've been told. It's a star player getting his ego bruised by a general manager who's not exactly known for his empathy in contract negotiations.

Is there a way to coexist? Is there a path back to some level of civility between Kucherov and Lightning management?

I don't know. But if I were to guess, I'd say Kucherov isn't traded before the deadline. If he still decides to walk, BriseBois can get something for his negotiating rights at the NHL draft. But I'm holding out hope that Kucherov and the Lightning find a way to mend fences and continue a successful and lucrative relationship.

Where else in the league is he going to celebrate a championship on a Jet Ski and give a beer-drenched shirtless news conference? That's Tampa, baby.

WINNERS AND LOSERS
Winner: Ryan Nugent-Hopkins
If you had told me back in 2016 that the Nuge would become the all-time leader in games played as an Oiler (1,038), there's zero chance I would have believed it. That was the year the Oilers offered Nugent-Hopkins to the Nashville Predators for defenseman Seth Jones, who was eventually traded to Columbus for Ryan Johansen.

I've said for years that Nuge is the kind of forward that teams trade away and then spend the next several seasons trying to find again. He's a versatile, hard-working "players' player."

I spoke with him on Tuesday, and it was clear that setting this mark for the Oilers meant everything to him.

"I haven't wavered throughout my entire career that I want to be an Edmonton Oiler. Start my career here, finish my career here," he said. "There's obviously sometimes you're not in control of that. I've been fortunate that I've been able to stick around and that they've had that faith in me."

Loser: Hometown Remix jerseys
We love the Hometown Remix jerseys. OK, most of the Hometown Remix jerseys.

Perhaps teams were overwhelmed by their sheer awesomeness, because those that wore their Remix jerseys through Wednesday night's games were just 4-5-2. Thursday night is the big test for this trend, as five teams will make their Remix debuts that evening.

Winner: Manitoban fish
Congratulations to the aquatic creatures of Manitoba, Canada, who were mentioned by Connor Hellebuyck in his Instagram "letter to fans" no less than five paragraphs before he mentioned any of his former Winnipeg Jets teammates.

Loser: #ArnielWatch
Logic dictated that Jets coach Scott Arniel would be out of a job right now. The Jets were winless in nine straight games, culminating in a 7-0 humiliation at the Carolina Hurricanes. At the end of a road trip, before a game against lowly Vancouver, the timing just seemed right.

And then the Jets set an NHL record with the latest four-goal comeback ever to stun the Canadiens, putting forth an effort in that game that might has saved Arniel's job.

"I really don't care about that. I really don't. I'm so happy that we won tonight," Arniel said when asked about the sword of Damocles hanging over him. "To me, we're still in the hunt."

Winner: Red Wings fans
Newly elected U.S. senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan? Puckhead. He was a hockey goalie in his youth sports days and a legit Detroit Red Wings fan.

"I was at the game when Darren McCarty took on Claude Lemieux," El-Sayed told the Octopus Thrower blog recently. "The '97 and '98 Stanley Cup championships are still highlights of my childhood. The teams the last few years have been a far cry from the Wings I came to love as a kid."

He also chimed in on the contract standoff between the Red Wings and one of their better young defensemen: "The team holding out on Simon Edvinsson is just the latest example in a long series of ownership prioritizing their bottom line over the team and the fans. Our teams aren't just assets for billionaires, they're part of our culture and heritage. Hockeytown deserves better."

Loser: Shawn Horcoff

The Red Wings interim general manager made it clear to suspended center Dylan Larkin: If you expand your list of approved trade destinations, there's a deal to be made.

But Larkin and agent Pat Brisson are holding it to the 10 approved teams. Larkin is willing to wait this out, probably with the hope that Horcoff swallows his pride and accepts that Minnesota offer.

FAVORITE OFF-ICE MOMENT
Have you seen this highlight from a recent University of North Dakota game?

Brad Elliott Schlossman, a fantastic writer for Grand Forks Herald, tracked down the fans involved: Jett Deren, 22, holding the beers and trying to get the attention of brother Cole, 28, who threw the blind elbow because he thought his little brother was bugging him.

In an effort to win a Pulitzer Prize, Schlossman got the brothers on a Zoom call for this story and just let'em rip:

Jett: "There was an older lady sitting two seats over to my left. I was like, oh my gosh, he got beer on an old lady. I felt so bad. She got a little bit. I thought she got more than she did. She looked over, saw it, and just gave it a quick little swipe off her shoulder."

Cole: "I apologized to her."

Jett: "A switch flipped."

Cole: "We were yelling at each other. Eventually, I realized, 'I've got to calm down. I just elbowed a whole beer onto this lady, the seat and my brother. I was in the wrong.'"

In the end, Cole admitted that he did take a little swig of what was left in the cup. As one does.

JERSEY FOUL OF THE WEEK

Alex Ovechkin has played in D.C. since 2005, and we've seen his name on several Washington football jerseys through the years.

There's something really honorific about Ovechkin being so iconic that he transcends all sports boundaries in D.C. But we're also fans of the punk rock subversion of having hockey on the jerseys of the most popular sport in America.

MUST-SEE GAMES

Anaheim Ducks at Edmonton Oilers

Thursday, Nov. 5, 8 p.m. ET

In their last six games, the Ducks are scoring a league high 4.67 goals per game while also giving up a league high 4.67 goals per game. And now they're playing Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl. Buckle up.

New Jersey Devils at Winnipeg Jets

Tuesday, Nov. 10, 8 p.m. ET

Connor Hellebuyck returns to Winnipeg. It might not reach the acidic heights of Brady Tkachuk Night in Ottawa but Jets fans will bring the bile.

PUCK HEADLINES
DATELINE: San Jose
The Sharks have been an massive disappointment this season, dropping to 7-9-1 with a thumping at the hands of the Los Angeles Kings on Wednesday night that resulted in a players' only meeting afterward.

We suspected their defense would be porous, given the inexperience on the roster, but not this porous: San Jose was last in the NHL in expected goals against and scoring chances against per 60 minutes through 16 games. But in projecting San Jose as a playoff team for the first time since 2019, we figured they could score their way out of defensive problems like the Ducks did last season. Alas, the Sharks were also last in 5-on-5 goals and expected goals for per 60 minutes, too.

GM Mike Grier hasn't made many missteps. Perhaps handing coach Ryan Warsofsky a multi-year extension in September, with one year left on his current deal, was one of them?

Here's a thought: If the Sharks flop this season and the coach takes the blame, is there a more logical landing spot for former Golden Knights coach Bruce Cassidy than behind the Sharks' bench? Vegas infamously holds his rights though next June, but he's free to sign anywhere after that. The structure, the gravitas, the pedigree ... if San Jose is treading water, Cassidy would get them swimming in the right direction.

But hopefully they don't flop. Warsofsky is a solid coach and it's still early. But the returns so far are pretty brutal.

DATELINE: World Cup of Hockey
Back in September, I spoke with NHL deputy commissioner Bill Daly about the Russia issue. We discussed this season's All-Star Game, in which five international teams will compete in a 3-on-3 tournament. That includes a "world" team for whom Russian players will be eligible to play.

"It's a league event. We shouldn't be excluding categories of players. Opening that up for Russians to be able to participate, I think it only made sense," he said.

Our conversation occurred right after the IOC executive board provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee. The NHL has certainly weighed the IOC's approach to Russia as a bellwether more than, say, the International Ice Hockey Federation. I asked Daly about that decision and its implications for events like the World Cup of Hockey in 2028, specifically when it comes to countries boycotting because Russia is in the tournament.

"I've been left with the understanding that if there's adequate cover, there's not going to be any issue with them participating," he told me.

That the NHL could point to the Olympics, say "Russians are allowed" and therefore the NHL must allow them too?

"That's what I've been led to believe," he said.

I thought of that conversation this week after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that the IIHF must lift its ban on Russian hockey teams that was in effect since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Again, that would seem like one of those "adequate cover" developments for the NHL and the NHLPA.

Except that ruling kicked the hornets' nest. Finland, Sweden, Czechia, Norway, Denmark and Latvia said they will not play games against Russia if the Russians are allowed into the IIHF world championship in Germany. The tournament's main sponsor, automaker Skoda, said it will "reassess" its involvement if Russia plays. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Russia will not be allowed to play at the upcoming IIHF world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

The next World Cup is scheduled for February 2028. A lot can change before then. But this week served as a reminder of how dug-in European teams are on Russian participation as long as their invasion continues. The Russia issue already helped scuttle one World Cup cycle. Hopefully that doesn't extend to 2028.

stories.headline: ESPN's AFL Misery Index: Which club would you have least wanted to support since 2000?
stories.summary: Which AFL club has had the most success since the turn of the century? Which teams' fans have had a miserable existence since 2000? We've ranked each club on our Misery Index.
stories.body:
Which AFL club would you have wanted to support most since the turn of the century? Of course, the answer to that question has to be your own team, but if we did get a second choice, who would you pick? In other words, which club has provided its fanbase with the most happiness? On the flip side, which team has provided the most disappointment?

Welcome to ESPN's AFL Misery Index.

This is a countdown of the teams that have given its fans with the least amount of joy since 2000. I'm not just looking at premierships and win percentages, but also finals records, droughts, off-field issues, as well as the ability to draft well and attract free agents.

Let's get into it, beginning with the team you would have most wanted to support!

18. Geelong
Record: 422-6-217 (65.9%)

Premierships: 4

Finals series/finals: 21/53

Bottom four finishes: 0

The Cats may not have won as many flags as the Lions in this period but what this club has going for it is sustained relevance and competitiveness since basically the turn of the century. Geelong just doesn't know how to be bad and if you're a fan born in 2000 you would have already witnessed your team win four premierships, play in seven Grand Finals, and feature in a staggering 15 preliminary finals. The Cats have also had more stability than anyone else, with just two coaches in the last 26 years. And to cap off the perfect supporter experience, Geelong is now just about the destination club for free agents and homesick Victorians.

17. Brisbane

Record: 331-6-297 (52.7%)

Premierships: 6

Finals series/finals: 14/41

Bottom four finishes: 8

Some will argue vehemently that it's insane to not have the Lions sitting top of this list given the club has won six premierships (and completed two separate three-peats) since 2000. Granted, that's more success than anyone else, and it's not particularly close. But between these two modern day dynasties, Brisbane was a complete rabble. In fact, the club featured in finals just once from 2005 to 2018 -- that's half of the period we're taking into consideration here! You'd love to have supported this mob, no doubt, but the Cats simply have to pip them for top spot based on their significantly higher floor.

16. Hawthorn
Record: 351-6-274 (56.1%)

Premierships: 4

Finals series/finals: 15/38

Bottom four finishes: 4

Of all the dynasties we've witnessed since the turn of the century, was Hawthorn's the best? There's a real argument to be made the dominance of this club, under Alastair Clarkson, tops anything else we've seen in recent times. The Hawks were the envy of the competition between 2008 and 2015, winning four flags with one of the greatest teams ever assembled. You'd be pretty thrilled going to the footy each week and watching both Lance Franklin and Cyril Rioli running around in your forward line! With Zach Merrett and Ben King being added to the mix this current offseason, Hawthorn is once again a premiership favourite.

15. Sydney
Record: 380-6-254 (59.8%)

Premierships: 2

Finals series/finals: 21/47

Bottom four finishes: 2

When you consider the Swans have played in seven of the last 21 Grand Finals and own the second-best win percentage since 2000, there's a strong argument they should rank higher on this list. But, of course, five of those Grand Finals ended in heartbreaking defeat. In the last two Grand Final losses, they've been belted off the park. That really stings! As does the recent Pullman Hotel saga involving a number of the club's most high-profile players. Still, there would be many footy fans selling their souls to the devil to have what the Swans have had this millennium.

14. Collingwood
Record: 361-8-267 (57.4%)

Premierships: 2

Finals series/finals: 17/43

Bottom four finishes: 4

The Magpies have provided their passionate fanbases with real bang for their supporter buck over the last 26 years. Of course, there's been six Grand Finals and two memorable triumphs, but also 17 finals series and 12 preliminary final appearances. Basically, just about one in every two years Collingwood is still alive at preliminary final weekend! The club has also avoided bottoming out and made a habit of immediately catapulting itself back up the ladder whenever they've suffered a down season. Say what you want about the Magpies army, but they've certainly experienced happiness since 2000.

13. Richmond
Record: 272-9-331 (45.2%)

Premierships: 3

Finals series/finals: 9/19

Bottom four finishes: 9

What an incredible four-year period it was for the Tigers between 2017 and 2020 where it played in three Grand Finals and won all three. Talk about capitalizing on your premiership window! From a fan perspective, the best part of the era might have been getting to watch three-time Norm Smith Medal winner and club legend Dustin Martin play each of his 302 games. However, outside of that dominant four-year block, Richmond managed to win just one final (in 2001) and finished in the bottom four on nine occasions, three times collecting the wooden spoon. Things also don't appear to be improving any time soon.

12. West Coast
Record: 291-4-327 (47.1%)

Premierships: 2

Finals series/finals: 14/29

Bottom four finishes: 9

Since 2000, the Eagles have played in four Grand Finals, winning two and losing two. Both flags were incredibly memorable. In 2006, West Coast got its revenge against Sydney, winning the thrilling decider by a solitary point. In 2018, they stormed over the top of Collingwood, a game that will forever be remembered for Dom Sheed's late brilliance in the pocket. Had it not been for an absolutely dire last five years -- arguably the worst 100-game stretch in the AFL era -- this club would probably have been in the top four. Still, Eagles fans continue to show up and support the club through its dark times.

11. Western Bulldogs
Record: 307-5-308 (49.9%)

Premierships: 1

Finals series/finals: 13/27

Bottom four finishes: 5

The Bulldogs are usually there or there abouts. A memorable breakthrough flag in 2016 provided so much joy to the loyal fanbase that had been starved of success for so long. They then returned to the Grand Final in 2021, losing to the Demons in the west. Before the Luke Beveridge era, the Bulldogs also enjoyed a strong patch under Rodney Eade, reaching three consecutive preliminary finals between 2008 and 2010. This club continues to employ Marcus Bontempelli, one of the greatest players of the generation, and just landed superstar midfielder Zak Butters. There's plenty to be chuffed about if you support the Dogs.

10. Port Adelaide
Record: 333-3-288 (53.6%)

Premierships: 1

Finals series/finals: 13/31

Bottom four finishes: 4

This club has played in two Grand Finals since the turn of the century. The first, in 2004, resulted in a premiership and denied Brisbane a fourth successive flag. The second, in 2007, resulted in the greatest loss in Grand Final history, a 119-point defeat at the hands of Geelong. Port Adelaide has not been back to the big dance since that day but under Ken Hinkley they were a picture of consistency for a decade, reaching four preliminary finals since 2014. Did you know that only Geelong, Sydney, Collingwood, and Hawthorn have won more games than the Power since 2000?

9. Adelaide
Record: 330-2-289 (53.3%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 14/29

Bottom four finishes: 4

The Crows have been average to decent for much of the last 26 years, which has to rank them somewhere in the middle. How does ninth sound?! This club has the best winning percentage since 2000 of teams that haven't won a premiership in the period, and sixth-best overall. They have also claimed three minor premierships in that time and outside of the shortened 2020 season haven't ever really had a bad year. But despite all of that, Adelaide has only featured in one Grand Final (where it started as a significant favourite and lost). That 2017 heartbreak against Richmond was followed by an infamous pre-season camp and seven-year September drought.

8. Melbourne
Record: 266-4-343 (43.7%)

Premierships: 1

Finals series/finals: 10/20

Bottom four finishes: 8

The 2021 premiership is doing plenty of heavy lifting for the Demons here. In fact, without that flag there's a real argument Melbourne should be on the bottom of this list. From 2005 to 2017 this club experienced the lowest of lows, routinely belted off the park and never coming close to playing finals. Who can ever forget that humiliating 186-point loss to the Cats in 2011 -- the second-greatest defeat in league history? But all (well, most) was forgotten with that breakthrough flag at Optus Stadium, though that in itself was a sore point for many of the Demons faithful who missed out on witnessing it in the flesh! The fact this club still hasn't won a final since that day is wildly disappointing.

7. Fremantle
Record: 304-3-308 (49.7%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 10/22

Bottom four finishes: 5

After this year's extraordinary Grand Final capitulation against Brisbane, maybe it wouldn't be outrageous for the Dockers to be at the bottom of this list. After all, has anything more demoralizing ever happened to a footy team on the field? I'm not so sure. It's now two Grand Finals Fremantle has played in and on both days they could probably consider themselves the better team. Yet the club still awaits its inaugural premiership. The fact the Dockers' list is in such a great spot right now, and is set up for the next half decade (at least) probably saves them from dropping a few more rungs here.

6. St Kilda
Record: 282-8-323 (46.7%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 9/20

Bottom four finishes: 6

Saints fans will argue they must be lower on this list, but remember, we're only talking from 2000 onwards. Since the turn of the century, this club has featured in three Grand Finals. Sure, one of them was a replay, and they were unable to win any of them, but simply being in those positions is far more than can be said for any of those ranking below them. What's incredibly tough to swallow for St Kilda supporters is seeing the club fall agonisingly short when they were competitive, a period which has been sandwiched by prolonged middling stretches. In other words, irrelevance.

5. GWS
Record: 164-4-180 (47.7%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 8/19

Bottom four finishes: 4

Remember when the media was convinced the Giants were going to win the next 10 premierships? Well, that aged like milk. GWS currently sits on zero flags, but the club did feature in the 2019 Grand Final, a day they were humiliated by Richmond. And then of course there was the home semifinal loss to eventual premier Brisbane in 2024, a game in which they led by 44 points. Oh, and the heartbreaking 2016 home preliminary final loss to the Bulldogs, another eventual premier. This club has had no shortage of talent but nothing to show for it. Its two best players, Jeremy Cameron and Toby Greene, have also both ultimately wanted to leave.

4. Essendon
Record: 276-7-328 (45.7%)

Premierships: 1

Finals series/finals: 11/18

Bottom four finishes: 8

Essendon's 2000 premiership might well have saved the club from last spot on this list, because since then they have basically lurched from one disaster to the next. There was heartbreak the following year with a Grand Final defeat to Brisbane, before three consecutive semifinal losses. The Bombers have now not won a final in 22 years, something that's become a meme in footy circles. Essendon also endured the biggest off-field saga this century with its involvement in the infamous supplements saga that led to coach sackings and player suspensions, setting the club back years. To cap it off, captain Zach Merrett begged to be traded, wasn't, and then was. Grim.

3. North Melbourne
Record: 256-5-349 (42.4%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 9/17

Bottom four finishes: 10

No team has finished in the bottom four more times since 2000 than North Melbourne. Even the 'good' periods were hardly worth celebrating, back-to-back preliminary final losses in 2014 and 2015 were followed by an elimination final loss in 2016 and then a dreadful, competition-worst 10-year finals drought. The Kangaroos have had nine coaches (Jaymie Graham will be the 10th) in the last 26 years and in many ways have forgotten what it feels like to win. The fact Nick Blakey is seen as the club's saviour proves attracting free agents and marquee signings has been slim pickings for this mob.

2. Carlton
Record: 242-6-362 (40.2%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 9/17

Bottom four finishes: 9

From the salary cap breach and draft pick punishment to a merry-go-round of coaches, there's been setback after setback for the Blues in the 21st century. This club has claimed a league-high five wooden spoons since 2000 (they had zero prior to 2000) and forced its fans to witness its most barren and disappointing stretch in history. The best moment in 26 years was a stirring semifinal win over Melbourne in 2023, which tells you all you need to know about how much this club has been starved of success in the modern era.

1. Gold Coast
Record: 114-2-237 (32.6%)

Premierships: 0

Finals series/finals: 1/2

Bottom four finishes: 9

Question: what's this club's greatest moment in history? Answer: a one-point win over Fremantle in an elimination final in 2025. Literally every other team has enjoyed a significantly higher peak this century, which has to place the Suns dead last on our ranking. That memorable final was one of just two finals Gold Coast has ever played and the only finals series it has qualified for (everyone else has at least eight in this time!). Season 2025 remains the only campaign in which the Suns won more games than they lost. Gold Coast also has easily the worst winning percentage of any club. Yeah, supporting this team has brought basically zero happiness.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton: Watching successor Kimi Antonelli win title 'highlight of my year'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton has said watching his Mercedes successor Kimi Antonelli win his first world championship was the "highlight" of his Formula 1 season.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton has said watching his Mercedes successor Kimi Antonelli win his first world championship was the "highlight" of his Formula 1 season.

Antonelli, who replaced the seven-time world champion at Mercedes at the start of 2025 following his move to Ferrari, clinched the title at Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest champion in F1 history at just 20 years old.

Hamilton, along with fellow multiple title-winner Max Verstappen, celebrated Antonelli's achievement on the podium and praised the Italian in a post on social media on Monday.

"Let me start with a huge congratulations to the new champion, Kimi Antonelli," Hamilton, 41, wrote on Instagram. "To have seen your journey so closely and to be there celebrating with you, was a highlight of my year. So well deserved and a record that will stand for a long time.

"It was great to see your team at Mercedes celebrating with you. Enjoy this moment, keep your family close, keep your passion and your energy."

Antonelli was just 18 when he stepped into Hamilton's seat at Mercedes, facing the daunting task of replacing the most successful driver in F1 history, who won six of his seven world titles with the Silver Arrows.

But the Italian has enjoyed a remarkable second season, beating teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Hamilton -- among others -- to the championship with four rounds still scheduled to take place.

Hamilton's congratulations came alongside an admission of frustration over Ferrari's weekend in Mexico, where he felt the team had missed an opportunity to win and also appeared to acknowledge tensions following Charles Leclerc's actions on the opening laps.

"Our own weekend was one full of challenges," Hamilton said. "We had a lot thrown at us but our mechanics and engineers did an incredible job.

"We've grown so much together this year, and that progress has taken a huge effort from everyone on the track and back at the factory. That's why losing what could've been a win hurts so much.

"We need to grasp every opportunity we have, so it's incredibly frustrating, and I can't pretend otherwise."

- Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari have 'big problems' after Charles Leclerc incident

- Hamilton demands 'serious talks' at Ferrari, questions Leclerc's 'mentality'

He added: "Battling is necessary, but when that battle costs the team, we have to be honest about it and learn from it.

"We can push each other to the limit and still honour the responsibility to everyone who put us on that track."

Despite his frustrations, Hamilton insisted his commitment to Ferrari remained unchanged.

"I'll keep giving everything I have. My belief in this team hasn't changed and neither has my responsibility to help us get this right," he said.

"Stick with us. I'm only just getting started with this team, and we have so much more to come."

stories.headline: MLS Power Rankings: Miami finds its feet with Decision Day coming up
stories.summary: Which teams are in the best position heading into Decision Day? All this and more in the latest edition of ESPN's MLS Power Rankings.
stories.body:
It's Monday and another weekend of action is in the books. With Decision Day coming up next week, it's time for the latest edition of ESPN's MLS Power Rankings to see which teams are in a good or bad spot to qualify for the MLS Cup playoffs.

1. Nashville SC
Previous ranking: 1

While seeking history on a rainy night in Tennessee, Nashville fell behind by two goals, had multiple goals called off, but battled back to force two own goals and clinch a 3-2 win against Red Bull New York with stoppage-time headed goal from Sam Surridge. The Supporters' Shield winners are level with Miami's points record, but could break it with just a point from their final game.

2. Inter Miami CF
Previous ranking: 2

Miami reclaimed second place in the Eastern Conference with a second-half rally against the Revs to win 2-1, ignited by the guy still leading the Golden Boot race: Lionel Messi. After a headed assist to Germán Berterame to level the score, Messi scored his 26th goal of the year after finagling past multiple defenders then sending a low left-footed strike past Matt Turner.

3. New England Revolution
Previous ranking: 4

The Revs' four-game win streak came to a halt against the Herons, as Messi proved the difference maker once more assisting and scoring in a come-from-behind win for Miami. With that, New England drops to third place in the Eastern Conference. Silver lining? Dániel Gazdag is now on a two-game scoring streak.

4. St. Louis City SC
Previous ranking: 3

STL had the firepower in the attacking third to come away with all three points against San Diego. But thanks in part to Pablo Sisniega's six saves and Anders Dreyer's moment of quality, they went home with a 1-0 defeat instead. The playoffs were already locked up but home-field advantage isn't as they head into the final weekend.

5. Chicago Fire
Previous ranking: 5

After going scoreless in six games, Robert Lewandowski came off the bench to make the difference in Colorado, providing the go-ahead goal 10 minutes after subbing on, then setting up Puso Dithejane for the 4-2 win.

6. Vancouver Whitecaps
Previous ranking: 7

The Whitecaps showed their quality in a comprehensive 5-1 dismantling of Seattle, highlighted by a Brian White brace that started in the 56th minute. After a 4-1 win over San Diego in midweek and 29th-place Montréal up next, the Western Conference's first-place side have got some momentum ahead of the postseason.

7. Philadelphia Union
Previous ranking: 6

After drawing Nashville 0-0 in the midweek, Philly's 1-0 loss to Cincinnati is their second in three games. They'll be in the postseason, but they may have a tough matchup when it comes.

8. FC Dallas
Previous ranking: 9

With the Golden Boot technically still in reach, Petar Musa (who scored 22 goals this season) missed his first penalty in six this season in the 97th minute. Stefan Cleveland's late-game save kept the Toros from three points in a 1-1 draw as they head into the final weekend looking to secure second place in the Western Conference.

9. LAFC
Previous ranking: 8

After losing 3-1 to Minnesota, LAFC are winless in three (two draws) ahead of a Decision Day battle with the Sounders. With their playoff place secure, they're competing for a better finish in the standings, but will fall short of their top-three finish in the Western Conference in the last four seasons.

10. Charlotte FC
Previous ranking: 13

Kristijan Kahlina, whose save percentage (75.9%) is second only to first-place Nashville's Brian Schwake (77.7%), stopped eight against Orlando in a match that ended 4-0 in Charlotte's favor, despite both teams firing off the same number of shots (and nearly the same on target, though Charlotte had higher quality opportunities).

11. Orlando City
Previous ranking: 11

After losing 4-0 to mid-table side Charlotte, Orlando picked up their first defeat in six games but still clinched their playoff spot based on other results. They're in the final wild card spot ahead of a final test against the Revs.

12. San Jose Earthquakes
Previous ranking: 15

The Quakes took 17 minutes to score twice against RSL, and that was enough to secure three points in a 2-1 win. That's their first win in six (four draws, one loss) as they look to secure their third-place spot in the Western Conference.

13. Seattle Sounders
Previous ranking: 10

In a 5-1 loss to Vancouver, Jordan Morris' brief light of life in the second half was overshadowed by the Whitecaps' rapid response in a match characterized by goalkeeper Andy Thomas looking painfully skyward for help from the scoreline. After losing to Houston in midweek, the Sounders have three defeats and no wins from their last five games. They play LAFC on the final day while sitting one place short of the wild card spots.

14. Colorado Rapids
Previous ranking: 14

Morgan Whittaker scored from close range to mark his third goal in three games and take an early 1-0 lead against Chicago. But at the end of a goal-heavy matchup, Lewandowski scored and assisted off the bench to help see the Fire to a 4-2 win. The Rapids ended the weekend in the final playoff position and have a tough final test against Dallas to hang on.

15. FC Cincinnati
Previous ranking: 17

Cincinnati only forced one save out of Andre Blake, but with the help of Roman Celentano's six stops, they booked their playoff spot with a 1-0 win against the Union. Ayoub Jabbari came off the bench in the second half and registered the sole tally of the night, capitalizing on Blake's save (a low-struck ball from Evander) to score off the rebound.

16. Houston Dynamo
Previous ranking: 16

The Dynamo could secure home advantage in the playoffs with a top-of-the-table finish, but are hanging on to fifth place ahead of the final day after losing 3-1 to Portland (their first loss in six). They have a decisive meeting with St. Louis on the final day, who are just ahead of them on goal difference but tied on points.

17. LA Galaxy
Previous ranking: 19

Sergi Roberto's first MLS goal was the icing on the cake of a 4-1 win against Austin that also featured Hirving Lozano's first goal back from injury and three assists from Marco Reus. Austin's not the toughest opponent in MLS this season, but the result matters as the Galaxy head into the final weekend still competing for a playoff spot.

18. Columbus Crew
Previous ranking: 20

The Crew may have lost the U.S. Open Cup final, but after beating D.C United 3-0, they're finishing the regular season on a five-game win streak. They confirmed their spot in the postseason and finished the weekend in one of the Eastern Conference's two wild card positions.

19. Portland Timbers
Previous ranking: 22

The Timbers secured a massive three points in a 3-1 win against the Dynamo highlighted by two assists and a goal from Vincent Janssen (nearly half his total goal contributions this year). With one game remaining, they're in a wild card spot and have one tentative hand on the playoffs.

20. Minnesota United
Previous ranking: 23

In his first start since September, Joaquín Pereyra powered the Loons to three points with two goals against LAFC in a 3-1 win. They're still short of a final playoff spot (by two points) but following this result, they can still potentially break in with a win (and other results going in their favor), with San Jose waiting on the final day.

21. Real Salt Lake
Previous ranking: 18

After falling behind 2-0 early to San Jose, Juan Manuel Sanabria's headed goal (his second of the year) in the 23rd minute provided life, but unfortunately nothing followed. They're currently outside the wild card spots ahead of a crucial final game against the Galaxy, but will also need some results to go their way.

22. Red Bull New York
Previous ranking: 12

RBNY had an early penalty stopped but came out with the upper hand against Nashville, taking a 2-0 lead in Tennessee that started with a beautiful link up between league wonderkids Adri Mehmeti and Julian Hall. But after two own goals and a stoppage-time winner from Nashville, the Red Bulls were eliminated from the playoffs in consecutive seasons for the first time ever.

23. New York City FC
Previous ranking: 21

After conceding a 91st-minute goal to last-placed Montréal, the Pigeons' playoff chances are officially over. A 1-1 draw isn't enough to launch them into the wild card position with one more game to go.

24. San Diego FC
Previous ranking: 26

Dreyer -- a back-to-back MLS All-Star -- won't feature in this year's postseason, but that didn't stop him from handing the recently-crowded U.S. Open Cup champions a loss in a 1-0 victory over St. Louis. Dreyer's left-footed chip from distance was a taste of quality we'll be missing seven days from now.

25. Austin FC
Previous ranking: 24

With no postseason hopes, victories must come from small achievements, like letting Reus assist three goals or having a goalkeeper make six saves while still conceding four.

26. Toronto FC
Previous ranking: 25

Toronto succumbed to a 3-1 defeat to Atlanta and ended their postseason dream in the process. Back to the drawing board for Robin Fraser's side, who showed signs of potential earlier in the season.

27. Sporting Kansas City
Previous ranking: 28

With the playoffs out of the picture and the all-time goals conceded in a single season record newly secured, SKC still did their best to sabotage Dallas by absconding with a 1-1 draw against a side looking to lock up their top-two finish in the Western Conference.

28. Atlanta United
Previous ranking: 29

Miguel Almirón won't appear in this year's playoffs, so he put on an end-of-season show in a 3-1 win against Toronto while eliminating the fellow Eastern Conference team from the playoffs. Five Stripes fans will take what they can get this year.

29. D.C. United
Previous ranking: 27

After losing to Toronto in the midweek, D.C. played Columbus with the playoffs already out of the picture and proceeded to lose 3-0. With 11 years since their last postseason victory, there's nowhere to go but up for this MLS original.

30. CF Montréal
Previous ranking: 30

It's too late to save their season, but not too late to sink somebody else's. A 91st-minute response to NYCFC's 1-0 lead secured their 26th point of the year and put to rest New York's postseason dream.

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Manly shut down Paseka enquiry, Cowboys keen on Savage
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is heating up as we move beyond November 1. Isaac Issa has news on Bradman Best's future and which clubs might be lining up a play for Sam Walker.
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is heating up as we move beyond November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Manly shut down Paseka enquiry
Manly have knocked back an enquiry from Canberra about Taniela Paseka's availability, with the Sea Eagles unwilling to release the prop.

ESPN understands the Raiders initiated the enquiry, contrary to reports Paseka had been shopped to the club.

While Manly are looking to move on Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor as they reshape their roster, Paseka is a player they want to retain.

The front-rower remains contracted to the Sea Eagles until the end of 2029.

Ricky Stuart has since publicly denied Canberra are pursuing Paseka.

Cowboys among clubs eyeing Savage

North Queensland are among the clubs showing interest in Canberra winger Xavier Savage, as rivals assess their recruitment options for 2028.

ESPN understands the Cowboys and a Sydney-based club are keeping tabs on the speedster, who is contracted to the Raiders until the end of 2027 and became eligible to negotiate with rivals on November 1.

Savage scored 13 tries in 19 NRL appearances for Canberra this season.

Bryenton begins Tigers chapter

David Bryenton will begin full-time training with the Wests Tigers on Wednesday, with ESPN understanding the recruit features in Benji Marshall's long-term plans.

Having first reported his signing last month, ESPN can reveal Bryenton's mutually agreed release from the Bulldogs has now been finalised, clearing the way for him to join Marshall's squad for pre-season.

Dolphins win race for Su'a

The Dolphins have won the race to retain Sebastian Su'a, with ESPN understanding the young forward has agreed to terms on a two-year extension that will keep him in Redcliffe until the end of 2029.

Several NRL clubs had identified Su'a as a potential recruitment target, but the Dolphins have moved to secure his future with the club.

Fa'alogo agrees to long-term Storm extension

Sua Fa'alogo has agreed to extend his stay at the Melbourne Storm through to the end of 2032, ESPN understands.

The agreement will keep the fullback in Melbourne for the next six seasons, securing a key figure in the Storm's long-term plans.

Fa'alogo's retention delivers a major boost for Melbourne ahead of the November 1 contracting window, with the club moving to lock down one of its most exciting talents.

Dolphins close in on Lemuelu extension, confident of keeping Farnworth

The Dolphins are closing in on a multi-year extension for Connelly Lemuelu as they also express confidence in retaining Herbie Farnworth.

ESPN understands Lemuelu is nearing an agreement to extend his stay despite interest from Canberra, Parramatta and Cronulla.

Securing the back-rower would deliver a retention boost for the Dolphins, with the length of the proposed deal yet to be confirmed.

The club is also understood to be confident it can retain Farnworth despite links to the Sydney Roosters.

While that confidence is yet to translate into a confirmed extension, keeping the English international alongside Lemuelu would help preserve key combinations on the Dolphins' left edge.

Eels edge ahead in Best race
Parramatta have emerged as the frontrunners to land Bradman Best, with multiple sources indicating the Newcastle centre is increasingly likely to join the Eels beyond 2027.

Best has been identified as a priority target for Parramatta, who are looking to bolster Jason Ryles' backline with an established representative star.

While a deal is yet to be confirmed, the Eels are understood to be in the box seat despite Newcastle's efforts to retain him with a lucrative extension.

Bulldogs unlikely to enter Walker race
